topics.title: All multiplication facts to 10×10: Recall facts for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10; use known facts to find related facts

questions.stem: Will the answer to \(\text{even} \times \text{even}\) be odd or even?
questions.hint: Test two simple examples of even × even and check whether the results end in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) or an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

keyPoints.note: Try two small number examples to verify the parity rule.

steps.explain: Choose a first pair of small numbers that match \(\text{even} \times \text{even}\) and calculate the result.
Check the last digit of the first result to see if it is even or odd. It is even.
Test a second pair of numbers to confirm the pattern always holds.
Both tests confirm the general rule: \(\text{even} \times \text{even}\) is always even.

questions.stem: Will the answer to \(\text{odd} \times \text{odd}\) be odd or even?
questions.hint: Test two simple examples of odd × odd and check whether the results end in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) or an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

keyPoints.note: Try two small number examples to verify the parity rule.

steps.explain: Choose a first pair of small numbers that match \(\text{odd} \times \text{odd}\) and calculate the result.
Check the last digit of the first result to see if it is even or odd. It is odd.
Test a second pair of numbers to confirm the pattern always holds.
Both tests confirm the general rule: \(\text{odd} \times \text{odd}\) is always odd.

questions.stem: Will the answer to \(\text{even} \times \text{odd}\) be odd or even?
questions.hint: Test two simple examples of even × odd and check whether the results end in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) or an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

keyPoints.note: Try two small number examples to verify the parity rule.

steps.explain: Choose a first pair of small numbers that match \(\text{even} \times \text{odd}\) and calculate the result.
Check the last digit of the first result to see if it is even or odd. It is even.
Test a second pair of numbers to confirm the pattern always holds.
Both tests confirm the general rule: \(\text{even} \times \text{odd}\) is always even.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(4 \times 3 = \square\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: We need to find 4 groups of 3.
Count by 3s four times: 3, 6, 9, 12.
Check with the turnaround fact 3 × 4 = 12.
Therefore, 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(3 \times \square = 12\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Use the inverse division fact to find the missing factor.
Count by 3s until you reach 12: 3, 6, 9, 12 (that is 4 steps).
Check by substituting 4 back into the equation: 3 × 4 = 12.
Therefore, the missing number is 4.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(3 \times 5 = \square\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: We need to find 3 groups of 5.
Skip-count by 5s three times: 5, 10, 15.
Check with the turnaround fact 5 × 3 = 15.
Therefore, 3 × 5 = 15.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(\square \times 3 = 15\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Use the inverse division fact to find the missing factor.
Skip-count by 3s up to 15: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 (5 steps).
Substitute 5 back into the equation to check: 5 × 3 = 15.
Therefore, the missing number is 5.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(6 \times 2 = \square\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Multiplying by 2 is the same as doubling the number.
Double 6: 6 + 6 = 12.
Check by counting by 2s six times: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
Therefore, 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(\square \times 6 = 12\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Use the inverse division fact: 12 ÷ 6.
Count by 6s to 12: 6, 12 (2 groups of 6).
Therefore, the missing number is 2.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(7 \times 4 = \square\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Multiplying by 4 is the same as doubling twice.
First double 7: 7 × 2 = 14.
Now double 14: 14 × 2 = 28.
Therefore, 7 × 4 = 28.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(4 \times \square = 28\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Use the inverse division fact: 28 ÷ 4.
Halve 28 twice to divide by 4: half of 28 is 14, half of 14 is 7.
Therefore, the missing factor is 7.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(9 \times 3 = \square\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Use the friendly fact 10 × 3 = 30 and subtract one group of 3.
Calculate 10 × 3 = 30.
Subtract 3 from 30: 30 - 3 = 27.
Therefore, 9 × 3 = 27.

questions.stem: Complete the number sentence: \(3 \times 9 = \square\). What number belongs in the box?
questions.hint: Remember that multiplication and division are inverse fact families — use a known multiplication fact to check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Use skip-counting or the inverse multiplication/division fact.

steps.explain: Use the commutative (turnaround) property: 3 × 9 equals 9 × 3.
Calculate 9 + 9 + 9: first 9 + 9 = 18.
Add the third 9: 18 + 9 = 27.
Therefore, 3 × 9 = 27.

questions.hint: Multiply each of the five numbers in Row 2 (10, 2, 8, 4, 7) by 3 one at a time.

keyPoints.note: Multiply each number in Row 2 (10, 2, 8, 4, 7) by 3.

steps.explain: Highlight Row 2 in the source grid: the five numbers are \(10, 2, 8, 4,\) and \(7\).

questions.stem: Split the larger number into tens and ones to multiply: \(6 \times 49\).
questions.hint: Split 49 into 40 + 9, multiply both parts by 6, then add the two products together.

keyPoints.text: Split the larger number into tens and ones

steps.explain: Split \(49\) into tens and ones: \(49 = 40 + 9\).

Add the two partial products together: \(240 + 54 = 294\).

questions.hint: Find the constant jump between consecutive numbers (-4) and apply it step by step to every blank.

keyPoints.note: Apply the constant step (-4) from one term to the next.

steps.explain: Identify the constant rule of the pattern: each term changes by \(-4\) from the previous term.

questions.stem: Sam’s mum uses \(6\) small hearts on \(1\) birthday cake (so \(12\) for \(2\) cakes, \(30\) for \(5\) cakes). How many small hearts are needed for \(3, 4,\) and \(6\) cakes?
questions.hint: Use the 6 times table: multiply 3 × 6, 4 × 6, and 6 × 6.

keyPoints.note: Multiply the number of cakes by 6.

steps.explain: Identify the rule from the pattern: 1 cake = 6, 2 cakes = 12, 5 cakes = 30, so multiply by 6.
Calculate for 3 cakes: \(3 \times 6 = 18\).
Calculate for 4 cakes and 6 cakes: \(4 \times 6 = 24\) and \(6 \times 6 = 36\).
Therefore, 18, 24, and 36 small hearts are needed.

questions.stem: Sam’s mum uses \(10\) cream beads on \(1\) birthday cake (so \(20\) for \(2\) cakes, \(60\) for \(6\) cakes). How many cream beads are needed for \(3, 4,\) and \(5\) cakes?
questions.hint: Use the 10 times table: multiply 3 × 10, 4 × 10, and 5 × 10.

keyPoints.note: Multiply the number of cakes by 10.

steps.explain: Identify the rule: each cake uses 10 cream beads (multiply by 10).

Calculate for 4 cakes and 5 cakes: \(4 \times 10 = 40\) and \(5 \times 10 = 50\).
Therefore, 30, 40, and 50 cream beads are needed.

questions.stem: Calculate \(5 \times 50\).

questions.stem: Use the split method to divide: \(84 \div 4\).
questions.hint: Split 84 into 80 + 4, divide both parts by 4, then add the two quotients.

steps.explain: Split \(84\) into tens and ones: \(84 = 80 + 4\).
Divide the tens part by \(4\): \(80 \div 4 = 20\).
Divide the ones part by \(4\): \(4 \div 4 = 1\).
Add the two quotients together: \(20 + 1 = 21\).

questions.stem: Use the split method to divide: \(96 \div 3\).
questions.hint: Split 96 into 90 + 6, divide both parts by 3, then add the two quotients.

steps.explain: Split \(96\) into tens and ones: \(96 = 90 + 6\).
Divide the tens part by \(3\): \(90 \div 3 = 30\).
Divide the ones part by \(3\): \(6 \div 3 = 2\).
Add the two quotients together: \(30 + 2 = 32\).

questions.stem: Use the split method to divide: \(63 \div 3\).
questions.hint: Split 63 into 60 + 3, divide both parts by 3, then add the two quotients.

steps.explain: Split \(63\) into tens and ones: \(63 = 60 + 3\).
Divide the tens part by \(3\): \(60 \div 3 = 20\).
Divide the ones part by \(3\): \(3 \div 3 = 1\).
Add the two quotients together: \(20 + 1 = 21\).

questions.stem: Using each of the digits \(5, 8,\) and \(4\) once, and using addition or multiplication, what is the largest number you can make?
questions.hint: Multiplying a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number beats adding or multiplying three 1-digit numbers. Compare 8 × 54 and 5 × 84 carefully!

keyPoints.note: Use 5, 8, and 4 once each; you can combine two digits into a 2-digit number.
Test the top multiplication combinations: 8 × 54 and 5 × 84.

steps.explain: Compare multiplying three 1-digit numbers against multiplying a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number. Making a 2-digit number gives a much larger product.

questions.hint: Draw a tree diagram with 2 base branches, and attach 3 topping branches to EACH base — then count all end branches (2 × 3).

Each base can pair with any of the 3 toppings (multiply 2 × 3).

questions.stem: How many strawberries does Su have if she has five times as many as Ria, who has ten strawberries?
questions.hint: "Five times as many as ten" means multiply 5 × 10.

keyPoints.note: "Five times as many as ten" means multiply 5 × 10.

steps.explain: Identify Ria’s amount (10 strawberries) and the multiplier (5 times as many).
Write the multiplication number sentence: 5 × 10.
Calculate 5 × 10 = 50.
Therefore, Su has 50 strawberries.

questions.stem: Ben ate two hamburgers every day for each day in June. How many hamburgers did he eat altogether?
questions.hint: Remember how many days are in June ("30 days hath September, April, June, and November"), then multiply by 2!

keyPoints.note: Remember how many days are in June ("30 days hath September, April, June, and November"), then multiply by 2!

steps.explain: Recall the number of days in the month of June: June has 30 days.
Ben ate 2 hamburgers each day, so write the number sentence 30 × 2.
Therefore, Ben ate 60 hamburgers altogether in June.

questions.stem: Megan started with eight figurines. She went to the market and bought some more. She now has triple the number of figurines she originally had. How many figurines does she have now?
questions.hint: "Triple" means 3 times as many. Multiply Megan’s starting number (8) by 3.

keyPoints.note: "Triple" means 3 times as many. Multiply Megan’s starting number (8) by 3.

steps.explain: Understand the word "triple": triple means multiplying by 3.
Write the multiplication number sentence using her original 8 figurines: 3 × 8.
Therefore, Megan now has 24 figurines.

questions.stem: One hundred elephants walked past the safari tourists. How many elephant feet went past?
questions.hint: Each elephant has 4 feet, so multiply 100 elephants by 4.

keyPoints.note: Each elephant has 4 feet, so multiply 100 elephants by 4.

steps.explain: Identify the hidden fact: every elephant has 4 feet.
Write the multiplication number sentence for 100 elephants: 100 × 4.
Multiply 4 by 100 by placing two zeros after 4: 400.
Therefore, 400 elephant feet went past.

questions.stem: Five giants ate four baked potatoes and five boiled potatoes each. How many potatoes were eaten altogether?
questions.hint: First add how many potatoes ONE giant ate (4 + 5 = 9), then multiply by 5 giants.

keyPoints.note: First add how many potatoes ONE giant ate (4 + 5 = 9), then multiply by 5 giants.

steps.explain: Find how many potatoes each individual giant ate: 4 baked + 5 boiled.
Multiply the 9 potatoes per giant by 5 giants.
Calculate 5 × 9 = 45 (or check: 5×4 = 20 and 5×5 = 25, then 20 + 25 = 45).
Therefore, 45 potatoes were eaten altogether.

questions.stem: There were \(21\) people at a party. One third of them ate five sausage rolls each. How many sausage rolls were eaten?
questions.hint: Step 1: Find one third of 21 people (21 ÷ 3 = 7). Step 2: Multiply those 7 people by 5 sausage rolls each.

keyPoints.note: Step 1: Find one third of 21 people (21 ÷ 3 = 7). Step 2: Multiply those 7 people by 5 sausage rolls each.

steps.explain: Find one third of 21 people by dividing 21 by 3.
Each of those 7 people ate 5 sausage rolls. Write the multiplication sentence: 7 × 5.
Calculate 7 × 5 = 35.
Therefore, 35 sausage rolls were eaten.

questions.stem: The volunteer at the charity shop is sorting the shoes. There are \(48\) shoes. How many pairs of shoes are there?
questions.hint: There are 2 shoes in every pair, so divide 48 by 2.

keyPoints.note: There are 2 shoes in every pair, so divide 48 by 2.

steps.explain: Recall that 1 pair of shoes equals 2 shoes.
Write the division number sentence: 48 ÷ 2.
Split 48 into 40 + 8 and halve each part: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 20 + 4 = 24.
Therefore, there are 24 pairs of shoes.

questions.stem: There are twenty-five chairs in the hall. When they are put away, they are stacked in fives. How many stacks of chairs will there be?
questions.hint: Divide the total number of chairs (25) by the number of chairs in each stack (5).

keyPoints.note: Divide the total number of chairs (25) by the number of chairs in each stack (5).

steps.explain: Identify the total chairs (25) and the size of each stack (5).
Write the division number sentence: 25 ÷ 5.
Use the inverse multiplication fact 5 × 5 = 25.
Therefore, there will be 5 stacks of chairs.

questions.stem: Tessa sorted her eighteen hairclips evenly into three containers. How many hairclips are in each container?
questions.hint: Share 18 hairclips equally among 3 containers by dividing 18 ÷ 3.

keyPoints.note: Share 18 hairclips equally among 3 containers by dividing 18 ÷ 3.

steps.explain: Identify the total hairclips (18) and the number of equal containers (3).
Write the division number sentence: 18 ÷ 3.
Use the inverse multiplication fact 3 × 6 = 18.
Therefore, there are 6 hairclips in each container.

questions.stem: Forty people from the care home are going to a concert. They are travelling in taxis, and each taxi can take five passengers. How many taxis do they need?
questions.hint: Divide the 40 people by 5 passengers per taxi (40 ÷ 5).

keyPoints.note: Divide the 40 people by 5 passengers per taxi (40 ÷ 5).

steps.explain: Identify the total people (40) and the capacity of each taxi (5).
Write the division number sentence: 40 ÷ 5.
Use the inverse multiplication fact 8 × 5 = 40.
Therefore, they need 8 taxis.

questions.stem: Thirty people are coming to May’s party. She is going to divide them into five equal groups to play a game. How many people will be in each group?
questions.hint: Divide 30 people equally into 5 groups: 30 ÷ 5.

keyPoints.note: Divide 30 people equally into 5 groups: 30 ÷ 5.

steps.explain: Identify the total number of people and the number of groups (or people per group).
Use the inverse multiplication fact to solve the division.
Check by multiplying the answer back.
Therefore, the answer is 6 people.

questions.stem: A class of thirty-two students is going to the zoo tomorrow. Only four students at a time can go into the gorilla enclosure. How many groups will it take for the whole class to see the gorillas?
questions.hint: Divide 32 students by 4 students per group: 32 ÷ 4.

keyPoints.note: Divide 32 students by 4 students per group: 32 ÷ 4.

steps.explain: Identify the total number of people and the number of groups (or people per group).
Use the inverse multiplication fact to solve the division.
Check by multiplying the answer back.
Therefore, the answer is 8 groups.

questions.stem: The baker packed \(9\) boxes with \(24\) cakes in each box. How many cakes did he pack altogether?
questions.hint: Multiply 9 × 24 by splitting 24 into 20 + 4: (9 × 20) + (9 × 4).

keyPoints.note: Equal groups in each box means multiply: 9 × 24.

steps.explain: Decide the operation: 9 equal boxes of 24 cakes each means multiplication (\(9 \times 24\)).
Split 24 into tens and ones: \(24 = 20 + 4\).
Multiply each part: \(9 \times 20 = 180\) and \(9 \times 4 = 36\).
Add the two partial products: \(180 + 36 = 216\) cakes.

questions.stem: Tina’s school is having a concert. They have set out \(85\) chairs altogether, with \(5\) chairs in each row. How many rows of chairs are there?
questions.hint: Divide 85 by 5 using the split method: 85 = 50 + 35, then (50 ÷ 5) + (35 ÷ 5).

keyPoints.note: Grouping 85 chairs into rows of 5 means divide: 85 ÷ 5.

steps.explain: Decide the operation: grouping 85 chairs into equal rows of 5 means division (\(85 \div 5\)).
Split 85 into two friendly multiples of 5: \(85 = 50 + 35\).
Divide each part by 5: \(50 \div 5 = 10\) and \(35 \div 5 = 7\).
Check: \(17 \times 5 = 85\). Therefore, there are 17 rows of chairs.
